questions.q: What does the `pure` keyword mean for a Solidity function, per this lesson?
options: The function neither reads nor writes any contract state at all
The function always costs zero gas even when writing state
The function can only be called by the contract's owner
The function must return a boolean
questions.explain: pure goes a step beyond view: a pure function works only with the values passed directly into it, without reading or writing any contract state.

questions.q: In the real checkAge contract, what does calling checkAge(17) actually return?
options: "You are not an adult"
"You are an adult"
An error
The number 17
questions.explain: Since 17 is less than 18, the else branch runs, returning "You are not an adult" — confirmed live in the demo.

questions.q: In the real `foo` function's chained if/else-if/else, what does calling foo(18) return?
options: 1, since 18 is not less than 10 but is less than 20
0, since 18 is less than 20
2, since 18 is the largest value tested
An error, since 18 falls between two conditions
questions.explain: The chain checks x < 10 first (false), then x < 20 (true, since 18 < 20), so it returns 1 — exactly as demonstrated live.

questions.q: What does the ternary expression `_x < 10 ? 1 : 2` actually mean?
options: If _x is less than 10, return 1 — otherwise, return 2
Always return 1
Always return 2
Return _x multiplied by 10
questions.explain: The ternary operator is shorthand for a simple if/else: the condition before the ?, the true-case value, then a colon, then the false-case value.

questions.q: What real-world analogy did the instructor use to introduce if/else logic?
options: A light switch: if it's on, the lights turn on; else, they stay off
A vending machine dispensing snacks
A bank vault with a combination lock
A traffic light changing colors
questions.explain: The instructor used the light-switch analogy: the condition is whether the switch is on, directly mirroring how an if/else check works in code.
